official_questions.stem: Which of the following is not a feature of the Money Bill ?
options: It can be introduced only in the Lower House.
It cannot be amended or rejected by the Upper House.
It can be introduced only on the recommendations of the President.
It can be rejected, approved or returned for reconsideration by the President.
official_questions.key: It can be rejected, approved or returned for reconsideration by the President.
official_questions.core_fact: A Money Bill is introduced only in Lok Sabha on the President's recommendation; Rajya Sabha can only make recommendations within 14 days; the President may assent or withhold assent but cannot return it for reconsideration.

statements.t: A Money Bill can be introduced only in the Lower House.
A Money Bill cannot be amended or rejected by the Upper House.
A Money Bill can be introduced only on the recommendation of the President.
statements.d: only on the recommendations of the President

statements.t: A Money Bill can be rejected, approved or returned for reconsideration by the President.
statements.fact: The President can give or withhold assent to a Money Bill but cannot return it for reconsideration (proviso to Art. 111 excludes Money Bills).

official_questions.rule: Money Bill: Lok Sabha only, President's recommendation, RS 14 days recommend-only, President assent/withhold – no return.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following is a “pocket veto” power in the Indian context ?
options: Speaker of Lok Sabha not allowing presentation of a bill
President keeping a bill pending with him, without any time limit and without approving
Prime Minister removing ministers from his Cabinet without any reason
Rajya Sabha vetoing the provisions of a bill approved by Lok Sabha
official_questions.key: President keeping a bill pending with him, without any time limit and without approving
official_questions.core_fact: Pocket veto: Art. 111 sets no time limit, so the President may keep a bill pending indefinitely, neither assenting, rejecting nor returning it (Zail Singh, Indian Post Office (Amendment) Bill 1986).

statements.t: Pocket veto in India means: Speaker of Lok Sabha not allowing presentation of a bill.
statements.fact: The Speaker has no veto; pocket veto is the President's.

statements.t: Pocket veto in India means: President keeping a bill pending with him, without any time limit and without approving.

statements.t: Pocket veto in India means: Rajya Sabha vetoing the provisions of a bill approved by Lok Sabha.
statements.fact: Rajya Sabha can reject an ordinary bill (deadlock -> joint sitting), which is not a pocket veto.

official_questions.rule: President: absolute, suspensive, pocket veto; no qualified veto; no pocket veto on Money/Constitution Amendment bills (Art. 368 must assent).

official_questions.core_fact: Art. 156(3)-(4): Governor holds office for five years but continues until his successor enters office; Art. 361: not answerable to any court; not answerable to the legislature or the Council of Ministers.

statements.t: The Governor is not answerable to either House of the State legislature.
statements.d: not answerable to either House of the State

statements.t: The Governor is not answerable to either House of Parliament.
statements.d: not answerable to either House of the Parliament

statements.t: The Governor is not answerable to the Council of Ministers.
statements.d: not answerable to Council of Ministers

statements.t: The Governor shall quit office immediately after expiry of his term.
statements.fact: The Governor continues after his 5-year term until his successor enters office (Art. 156(4)).

official_questions.rule: Governor: 5 years, at President's pleasure, holds over till successor; same for President (Art. 56(1)(c)).

official_questions.stem: The orders passed by the Governor of a State (Article 163) of a State fall in four categories. Find out the category which is not subject to Judicial Review.
options: The exercise of executive power in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution by or under the order of the Governor
Orders passed by the Governor on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister
Where the Governor acts without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers and acts in his own discretion
official_questions.key: Where the Governor acts without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers and acts in his own discretion
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 163(2): the validity of anything done by the Governor in his discretion shall not be called in question on the ground that he ought or ought not to have acted in his discretion; orders on ministerial advice and pardons (Epuru Sudhakar 2006) are reviewable.

statements.t: Among the Governor's orders, the category not subject to judicial review is: The exercise of executive power in accordance with the provisions of the Constitution by or under the order of the Governor.
statements.fact: Executive acts under the Constitution are reviewable.

statements.t: Among the Governor's orders, the category not subject to judicial review is: Orders passed by the Governor on the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers headed by the Chief Minister.
statements.fact: Orders on ministerial advice are reviewable like any executive action.

statements.t: Among the Governor's orders, the category not subject to judicial review is: Orders like grant of pardon.
statements.fact: Pardons under Art. 161 are reviewable on limited grounds (Epuru Sudhakar 2006).

statements.t: Among the Governor's orders, the category not subject to judicial review is: Where the Governor acts without the aid and advice of the Council of Ministers and acts in his own discretion.

official_questions.rule: Art. 163(2) shields discretion; but Nabam Rebia (2016) limited discretion to Constitution-specified cases; pardons reviewable on mala fides/arbitrariness.
official_questions.key_note: Nabam Rebia (2016) and Rameshwar Prasad (2006) show that discretionary acts are not wholly beyond review (mala fides, extraneous grounds); key reflects Art. 163(2) text.

official_questions.stem: Regarding the Union Council of Council of Ministers, choose the wrong answer.
options: A Council of Ministers must always exist to advise the President.
Even after the dissolution of Lok Sabha, Council of Ministers exists to advise the President.
Even after the resignation of the Prime Minister, Council of Ministers exists to advise the President.
During the period of National Emergency, the President acquires discretionary powers, and can take independent decisions.
official_questions.key: During the period of National Emergency, the President acquires discretionary powers, and can take independent decisions.
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 74(1): there shall be a Council of Ministers to aid and advise the President, who shall act on its advice (42nd/44th Amendments); it continues after LS dissolution (U.N.R. Rao 1971) and until a new one; no extra discretion arises in an Emergency.

statements.t: A Council of Ministers must always exist to advise the President.
Even after dissolution of the Lok Sabha, the Council of Ministers exists to advise the President.
statements.d: after the dissolution of Lok Sabha

statements.t: Even after the PM resigns, the Council of Ministers continues to advise the President.
statements.d: after the resignation of the Prime Minister

statements.t: During a National Emergency the President acquires discretionary powers and can take independent decisions.
statements.fact: Even in a National Emergency the President acts on ministerial advice (Art. 74); the Emergency is itself proclaimed on Cabinet's written advice (Art. 352(3)).

official_questions.rule: President acts on advice always (Art. 74(1)); may ask once for reconsideration; Emergency adds Union powers, not presidential discretion.

official_questions.stem: Regarding the disagreement between the two Houses of the State Legislature, which of the following is correct ?
options: The bill ends and becomes dead
To resolve the issue a joint sitting will be called for
The only power of the Council is to interpose some delay in the passage of the bill
Legislative Council is a resolving body like Rajya Sabha
official_questions.key: The only power of the Council is to interpose some delay in the passage of the bill
official_questions.core_fact: No joint sitting in States; on an ordinary bill the Council can delay up to 3 months the first time and 1 month the second; the Assembly's version then prevails (Art. 197).

statements.t: On a disagreement between the two Houses of a State Legislature: The bill ends and becomes dead.
statements.fact: The bill does not die; the Assembly prevails after the delay.

statements.t: On a disagreement between the two Houses of a State Legislature: To resolve the issue a joint sitting will be called for.
statements.fact: Joint sittings exist only for Parliament (Art. 108), not States.

statements.t: On a disagreement between the two Houses of a State Legislature: The only power of the Council is to interpose some delay in the passage of the bill.
On a disagreement between the two Houses of a State Legislature: Legislative Council is a resolving body like Rajya Sabha.
statements.fact: The Council is weaker than Rajya Sabha and not a resolving body.

official_questions.rule: State: Council delay max 4 months (3+1), Money Bill 14 days; no joint sitting.

official_questions.stem: Choose the correct answer from the following :
options: A member of an All India Service can be dismissed or removed only by the Union government.
A member of an All India Service can be dismissed or removed only by the State government also if he serving under the State.
In India, State Government employees administer State laws only.
Union Government through its departments administers Union laws.
official_questions.key: A member of an All India Service can be dismissed or removed only by the Union government.
official_questions.core_fact: AIS officers are recruited and appointed by the Centre (President); though serving States, they can be dismissed or removed only by the Union government (Art. 311, AIS Act 1951); Union laws are largely executed by State machinery (Arts 256-258).

statements.t: A member of an All India Service can be dismissed or removed only by the Union government.
A member of an AIS serving under a State can be dismissed or removed by the State government also.
statements.fact: The State can suspend/discipline but not dismiss or remove an AIS officer.

statements.t: In India, State government employees administer State laws only.
statements.fact: State employees also administer many Union laws (integrated administration, Arts 256-258).

statements.t: The Union government administers Union laws through its departments.
statements.fact: Union laws are mostly executed through State machinery, not only through Union departments.

official_questions.rule: AIS: Centre appoints/removes; State controls posting/suspension; India's integrated administration (unlike US dual machinery).

official_questions.stem: Regarding the powers of the President, which of the following is correct ?
options: No previous sanction is required or recommendation of the President for introducing any legislation on any matter.
Courts are debarred from invalidating any legislation on the ground that the President's previous sanction was not obtained.
A money bill can be returned for re-consideration.
President does not have the power of disallowance of a bill of the State legislature, which may have been reserved for his consideration by the Governor of the State.
official_questions.key: Courts are debarred from invalidating any legislation on the ground that the President's previous sanction was not obtained.
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 255: no Act is invalid merely because a required recommendation or previous sanction was not given, if assent was later given by the Governor/President; the President cannot return a Money Bill; he can withhold assent to (disallow) a reserved State bill (Art. 201).

statements.t: No previous sanction or recommendation of the President is required for introducing any legislation on any matter.
statements.d: No previous sanction is required ... any matter
statements.fact: Several bills need prior sanction/recommendation (Arts 3, 117, 274, 304(b)).

statements.t: Courts are debarred from invalidating legislation on the ground that the President's previous sanction was not obtained.
A Money Bill can be returned for reconsideration.
statements.fact: A Money Bill cannot be returned for reconsideration.

statements.t: The President has no power of disallowance of a State bill reserved for his consideration.
statements.d: does not have the power of disallowance
statements.fact: The President can withhold assent to a reserved State bill (Art. 201) – an absolute disallowance power.

official_questions.rule: Prior sanction needed: Art. 3, 117, 274, 304(b); defect cured by later assent (Art. 255).

official_questions.stem:
Match the following :
a. Reprieve — I. Reduce the amount of sentence without changing its character
b. Respite — II. Substitute one form of punishment for other of a lighter character
c. Remission — III. Awarding lesser sentence
d. Commutation — IV. A stay of execution of sentence
Codes :
a b c d
official_questions.core_fact: Reprieve = stay of execution of sentence; respite = lesser sentence due to special facts (pregnancy, disability); remission = reduce quantum without changing character; commutation = substitute a lighter form of punishment; pardon = absolve fully.

statements.t: Reprieve - a stay of execution of sentence.
Respite - awarding a lesser sentence.
Remission - reduce the amount of sentence without changing its character.
Commutation - substitute one form of punishment for another of a lighter character.
Reprieve - reduce the amount of sentence without changing its character.
statements.fact: Reprieve = stay of execution; reducing quantum = remission.

statements.t: Reprieve - awarding a lesser sentence.
statements.fact: Reprieve = stay of execution; lesser sentence = respite.

statements.t: Respite - reduce the amount of sentence without changing its character.
statements.fact: Respite = lesser sentence; reducing quantum = remission.

statements.t: Respite - substitute one form of punishment for another.
statements.fact: Respite = lesser sentence; substituting a form = commutation.

statements.t: Remission - substitute one form of punishment for another.
statements.fact: Remission = reduce quantum; substituting form = commutation.

statements.t: Remission - awarding a lesser sentence.
statements.fact: Remission = reduce quantum; lesser sentence for special reason = respite.

statements.t: Commutation - reduce the amount of sentence without changing its character.
statements.fact: Commutation = substitute lighter form; reducing quantum = remission.

statements.t: Commutation - a stay of execution of sentence.
statements.fact: Commutation = substitute lighter form; stay = reprieve.

official_questions.rule: Re-PRIEVE = PAUSE (stay); reSPITE = Special reason lesser; reMISSION = Minus quantity; COMMUTATION = Change form.

official_questions.stem: Regarding the pardoning powers, choose the correct answer.
options: Under the Indian Constitution, the pardoning power of the President and Governor are one and the same.
For offences made under Concurrent lists, without the State role, President alone has the pardoning power.
The only authority for pardoning a sentence of death is the President.
As regards suspension, remission, the Governor does not have a concurrent jurisdiction with the President.
official_questions.key: The only authority for pardoning a sentence of death is the President.
official_questions.core_fact: Only the President can pardon a death sentence and court-martial sentences; the Governor can suspend, remit or commute a death sentence; for Concurrent List offences both have power; President's power is wider than the Governor's.

statements.t: The pardoning powers of the President and the Governor are one and the same.
statements.fact: The President's power is wider (court martial, death-sentence pardon).

statements.t: For offences under Concurrent List laws, the President alone has the pardoning power.
statements.fact: For Concurrent List offences both President and Governor have pardoning power.

statements.t: The only authority for pardoning a sentence of death is the President.
statements.d: only authority for pardoning a sentence of death

statements.t: As regards suspension and remission, the Governor does not have concurrent jurisdiction with the President.
statements.d: does not have a concurrent jurisdiction
statements.fact: The Governor has concurrent power to suspend, remit or commute (even a death sentence).

official_questions.rule: President: court martial + death pardon; Governor: can commute/remit death but not pardon; both for State/Concurrent offences.

official_questions.stem: A sitting of the Parliament can be terminated by adjournment, prorogation or dissolution. In this regard choose the correct answer.
options: Adjournment terminates sitting as well as session of the House.
All pending notices including introducing bills lapse on prorogation.
Dissolution ends all business including bills and motions before the Lok Sabha.
Adjournment sine die means terminating a sitting for an indefinite period.
official_questions.key: Adjournment sine die means terminating a sitting for an indefinite period.
official_questions.core_fact: Adjournment ends a sitting, not the session; adjournment sine die ends a sitting without fixing a day; prorogation ends the session – pending notices (other than for introducing bills) lapse but bills do not; dissolution lapses most LS business, with exceptions (bills pending in RS not passed by LS, notified joint-sitting bills).

statements.t: Adjournment terminates the sitting as well as the session of the House.
statements.d: terminates sitting as well as session
statements.fact: Adjournment ends only the sitting, not the session.

statements.t: All pending notices including those for introducing bills lapse on prorogation.
statements.fact: On prorogation pending notices lapse except notices for introducing bills; bills do not lapse.

statements.t: Dissolution ends all business including bills and motions before the Lok Sabha.
statements.fact: Dissolution lapses most business, but not bills pending in RS that LS has not passed, or bills notified for a joint sitting.

statements.t: Adjournment sine die means terminating a sitting for an indefinite period.

official_questions.rule: Adjournment = sitting (by presiding officer); prorogation = session (President), bills survive; dissolution = LS only, most bills lapse.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following bodies concerned with Inter-State relations are Constitutional ?
official_questions.core_fact: The Inter-State Council is constitutional (Art. 263); river water tribunals are statutory (Inter-State River Water Disputes Act 1956 under Art. 262); Zonal Councils statutory (SRA 1956).

statements.t: The River Water Tribunal is a constitutional body concerned with inter-State relations.
statements.fact: River water tribunals are statutory (1956 Act), though Art. 262 enables the law.

statements.t: The Inter-State Council is a constitutional body concerned with inter-State relations.
The Zonal Council is a constitutional body concerned with inter-State relations.
statements.fact: Zonal Councils are statutory (SRA 1956).

statements.t: The Zonal Tribunals is a constitutional body concerned with inter-State relations.
statements.fact: There are no 'Zonal Tribunals'.

official_questions.rule: Constitutional: ISC (263); statutory: Zonal Councils (1956), water tribunals (1956 Act), NE Council (1971).

official_questions.stem: M.M. Punchhi Committee was appointed to study Centre-State relations. Regarding Punchhi recommendations all the following statements are correct except
options: Localising the Emergency Provisions under Articles 355 and 356 either to district or part of district.
Deployment of Central forces without State's consent for a short period.
In appointing the Chief Minister, pre-poll alliance should be treated as one political party.
National Integration Commission shall meet once in two years
official_questions.key: National Integration Commission shall meet once in two years
official_questions.core_fact: Punchhi (2010): localise emergency (Arts 355/356) to a district or part; Centre may deploy forces without State consent for a short period; pre-poll alliance to be treated as one party for CM appointment; National Integration Council to meet at least once a year.

statements.t: Punchhi recommended localising emergency provisions under Arts 355/356 to a district or part of a district.
Punchhi recommended deployment of central forces without the State's consent for a short period.
Punchhi recommended that a pre-poll alliance be treated as one party in appointing the CM.
Punchhi recommended that the National Integration Council meet once in two years.
statements.fact: Punchhi wanted the National Integration Council to meet at least once a year.

official_questions.rule: Punchhi: localised emergency, short-term central forces, pre-poll alliance = one party, NIC yearly, Governor removal via State resolution.
official_questions.key_note: Stem/option say 'National Integration Commission'; the body is the National Integration Council.

official_questions.stem: Regarding the composition of the Legislative Council, all following statements are correct, except
options: 1/3rd of the total number of Council shall be elected from local bodies.
1/12th of the total number of Council shall be elected by graduates.
1/12th of the total number of Council shall be elected by Teachers.
1/13th of the total number of Council shall be elected by Legislative Assembly.
official_questions.key: 1/13th of the total number of Council shall be elected by Legislative Assembly.
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 171(3): 1/3 elected by local bodies, 1/12 by graduates, 1/12 by teachers, 1/3 by MLAs, 1/6 nominated by Governor.

statements.t: One-third of the Council is elected by local bodies.
One-twelfth of the Council is elected by graduates.
One-twelfth of the Council is elected by teachers.
One-thirteenth of the Council is elected by the Legislative Assembly.
statements.fact: One-third (not 1/13) is elected by MLAs.

official_questions.rule: MLC: 1/3 MLAs + 1/3 local bodies + 1/12 graduates + 1/12 teachers + 1/6 nominated; size <= 1/3 of Assembly, >= 40.

official_questions.stem: The President may appoint a Governor of a State as the administrator of an adjoining Union Territory. Such Governor in the administration of Union Territory shall exercise his functions
options: On the aid and advice of his Council of Ministers.
As such administrator independently of his Council of Ministers.
Governor can form his choice of Council of Ministers for aid and advice.
A Governor of a State cannot be appointed as an Administrator of a Union Territory.
official_questions.key: As such administrator independently of his Council of Ministers.
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 239(2): the President may appoint a State Governor as administrator of an adjoining UT; he then acts independently of his Council of Ministers.

statements.t: A Governor appointed administrator of an adjoining UT exercises his functions: On the aid and advice of his Council of Ministers.
statements.d: aid and advice of his Council of Ministers
statements.fact: His State ministers have no role in the UT (Art. 239(2)).

statements.t: A Governor appointed administrator of an adjoining UT exercises his functions: As such administrator independently of his Council of Ministers.
statements.d: independently of his Council of Ministers

statements.t: A Governor appointed administrator of an adjoining UT exercises his functions: Governor can form his choice of Council of Ministers for aid and advice.
statements.d: form his choice of Council of Ministers
statements.fact: He cannot form a separate Council of Ministers for the UT.

statements.t: A Governor appointed administrator of an adjoining UT exercises his functions: A Governor of a State cannot be appointed as an Administrator of a Union Territory.
statements.fact: Art. 239(2) expressly allows it (e.g. Punjab Governor = Chandigarh administrator).

official_questions.rule: Punjab Governor administers Chandigarh – independently of Punjab ministers.

official_questions.stem: Parliament has the power to enact laws with respect to a matter in the State list in the national interest. In this regard choose the wrong answer.
options: On the request of two or more States.
Legislation for giving effect to International agreements.
Both Union and State governments have absolute freedom to make laws related to Concurrent list.
Inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and laws made by the Legislatures of States.
official_questions.key: Both Union and State governments have absolute freedom to make laws related to Concurrent list.
official_questions.core_fact: Parliament may legislate on State matters on the request of two or more States (Art. 252) and to implement international agreements (Art. 253); on Concurrent subjects a Central law prevails on inconsistency (Art. 254) – no 'absolute freedom'.

statements.t: Parliament can legislate on a State matter on the request of two or more States.
statements.d: request of two or more States

statements.t: Parliament can legislate on a State matter to give effect to international agreements.
Both Union and State governments have absolute freedom to make laws on the Concurrent List.
statements.fact: On Concurrent subjects a Union law prevails over a repugnant State law (Art. 254); there is no absolute freedom.

statements.t: The Constitution provides for inconsistency between laws made by Parliament and State legislatures (Art. 254).

official_questions.rule: State List entry by Parliament: 249 (RS), 250 (emergency), 252 (2+ States), 253 (treaty), 356 (PR); Concurrent: Union prevails (254) unless President's assent to State law.

official_questions.stem: State Government can pass a law imposing restrictions on goods imported from other States. Such law shall be moved in the Legislature of a State without the previous sanction of the
official_questions.core_fact: Proviso to Art. 304(b): a bill imposing reasonable restrictions on trade with other States can be introduced in a State legislature only with the President's previous sanction.

statements.t: A State law imposing restrictions on goods imported from other States can be moved only with the previous sanction of the Governor.
statements.fact: Sanction is the President's, not the Governor's.

statements.t: A State law imposing restrictions on goods imported from other States can be moved only with the previous sanction of the President.
A State law imposing restrictions on goods imported from other States can be moved only with the previous sanction of the Union Government.
statements.fact: Constitution names the President, not 'Union Government'.

statements.t: A State law imposing restrictions on goods imported from other States can be moved only with the previous sanction of the Inter-State Council.
statements.fact: ISC is advisory, has no sanction role.

official_questions.rule: Previous sanction of President: Art. 304(b) State trade restrictions; Art. 3 needs his recommendation.

official_questions.stem:
Which of the following statements is correct with respect to the State Finance Commission ?
I. It is required to appoint a State Finance Commission once in five years.
II. It recommends the determination of taxes, duties, tolls and fees assigned to the Panchayats and Municipalities.
III. Article 243 deals with constitution of finance commission to review financial position of Panchayats.
Choose the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 243-I (Panchayats) and 243-Y (Municipalities): the Governor constitutes a State Finance Commission every five years to review finances and recommend distribution and assignment of taxes, duties, tolls and fees and grants.

statements.t: A State Finance Commission is to be appointed once in five years.
The SFC recommends the determination of taxes, duties, tolls and fees assigned to Panchayats and Municipalities.
Article 243 deals with constitution of a finance commission to review the financial position of Panchayats.

official_questions.rule: SFC: 243-I (Panchayats), 243-Y (Municipalities); Union FC: Art. 280.
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only. Statement III is loose: the provision is Article 243-I (Article 243 is definitions). Options also mention a non-existent statement IV. Key kept.

official_questions.stem:
Consider the following Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and choose the correct code :
Assertion (A) :
The President is the executive power of the Union.
Reason (R) :
The executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and shall be exercised by him either directly or through officers subordinate to him in accordance with the Constitution.
Code :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
official_questions.key: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 53(1): the executive power of the Union is vested in the President and exercised by him directly or through subordinate officers in accordance with the Constitution.

statements.t: The President is the executive power of the Union.
The executive power of the Union shall be vested in the President and exercised by him directly or through subordinate officers.
R (Art. 53) explains A.

official_questions.rule: Art. 53 Union executive -> President; Art. 154 State executive -> Governor; real power with ministers (Art. 74).

official_questions.stem: Which of the following statements is not one of the powers of the Speaker of the Legislative Assembly ?
options: He has no veto except in case of a tie.

A Speaker may be removed from office by a resolution of the Assembly passed by a majority of all the then members of the Assembly after fourteen days notice of the intention to move such a resolution.
The Speaker vacates his office if he ceases to be a member of the Assembly.
The Speaker will preside when a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration of the Assembly.
official_questions.key: The Speaker will preside when a resolution for his removal from office is under consideration of the Assembly.
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 189: Speaker has only a casting vote in a tie; Art. 179: vacates on ceasing to be a member, removable by resolution passed by a majority of all the then members after 14 days' notice; Art. 181: shall not preside while his removal resolution is under consideration (may speak and vote in first instance).

statements.t: The Speaker has no vote except a casting vote in case of a tie.
statements.d: no veto except in case of a tie

statements.t: A Speaker may be removed by a resolution passed by a majority of all the then members after 14 days' notice.
statements.d: majority of all the then members

statements.t: The Speaker vacates office if he ceases to be a member of the Assembly.
The Speaker will preside when a resolution for his removal is under consideration.
statements.fact: Art. 181: he shall not preside while his removal resolution is under consideration.

official_questions.rule: Speaker under removal: cannot preside, can speak and vote in first instance (not casting vote) – Arts 96/181.
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only. Option 1 says 'veto' – evidently 'vote'.

official_questions.stem:
Consider the following Assertion (A) and Reason (R) and choose the correct code :
Assertion (A) :
The Parliament of India consists of the President and two Houses.
Reason (R) :
The President is a part of the legislature even though he does not sit in Parliament except for the purpose of delivering his opening address.
Code :
options: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).
official_questions.key: Both (A) and (R) are true and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
official_questions.core_fact: Art. 79: Parliament consists of the President and two Houses; the President is integral to legislation (assent, summoning, addresses under Art. 87) though he does not sit in either House.

statements.t: The Parliament of India consists of the President and two Houses.
The President is part of the legislature though he does not sit in Parliament except to deliver his address.
R explains A.

official_questions.rule: Parliament = President + RS + LS; State Legislature = Governor + House(s) (Art. 168).
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following entries of the Indian Constitution deals with the institutions for scientific or technical education financed by the Government of India, wholly or in part, and declared by Parliament, by law to be institutions of national importance ?
official_questions.core_fact: List I: Entry 63 – BHU, AMU, Delhi University and other institutions of national importance by law; Entry 64 – scientific/technical education institutions financed by GoI and declared of national importance; Entry 65 – Union agencies for training, research, crime investigation; Entry 66 – coordination and determination of standards in higher education.

statements.t: Entry 64 of the Union List deals with GoI-financed scientific/technical institutions of national importance.
Entry 63 of the Union List deals with GoI-financed scientific/technical institutions of national importance.
statements.fact: Entry 63 covers named universities (BHU, AMU, DU).

statements.t: Entry 65 of the Union List deals with GoI-financed scientific/technical institutions of national importance.
statements.fact: Entry 65 covers Union agencies for professional training and research.

statements.t: Entry 66 of the Union List deals with GoI-financed scientific/technical institutions of national importance.
statements.fact: Entry 66 covers standards in higher education.

official_questions.rule: List I: 63 universities, 64 technical institutes, 65 training agencies, 66 standards; education generally – List III Entry 25 (since 42nd).
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only.

official_questions.stem: Who said “India is not a nation in the traditional western sense but a comprehensive culture of continental scope compounded of a very large number of linguistic and religious entities, highly complex and often strongly antagonistic local cultures” ?
official_questions.core_fact: The quotation describing India as 'a comprehensive culture of continental scope ... not a nation in the traditional western sense' is attributed (per key) to Carl J. Friedrich.

statements.t: Carl Friedrich said India is not a nation in the traditional western sense but a comprehensive culture of continental scope.
P.H. Appleby said India is not a nation in the traditional western sense but a comprehensive culture of continental scope.
statements.fact: Key credits Carl Friedrich; Appleby wrote reports on Indian public administration (1953, 1956).

statements.t: Woodrow Wilson said India is not a nation in the traditional western sense but a comprehensive culture of continental scope.
statements.fact: Key credits Carl Friedrich; Wilson wrote on public administration (1887).

statements.t: Jawaharlal Nehru said India is not a nation in the traditional western sense but a comprehensive culture of continental scope.
statements.fact: Key credits Carl Friedrich; Nehru's 'unity in diversity' theme differs.

official_questions.rule: Federalism theorists: Wheare (quasi-federal), Friedrich (federalism as process), Ivor Jennings (strong centralising tendency), Granville Austin (cooperative federalism).
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only; attribution not independently verified.

official_questions.stem:
Which of the following statement/statements is/are valid regarding the office of the 'Whip' ?
I. Although not mentioned in the Constitution of India, the office of the 'Whip' has however been incorporated in the Rules of the House by the 'Leaders and Chief Whips of Recognised Parties and Groups in Parliament (Facilities) Act, 1998'.
II. The role of the Chief Whip of the government party in the Lok Sabha is served by the Minister of State for Parliamentary Affairs.
III. All political parties - whether ruling or opposition, will have their own Whips in the Parliament.
IV. The Chief Whip is not responsible to the leader of the House but is responsible only to the leader of the party that has appointed him/her to the office of Chief Whip.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: The office of Whip is not mentioned in the Constitution, the Rules of the House or a parliamentary statute; it rests on conventions (the 1998 Facilities Act only gives facilities). Every party has its whip; the government Chief Whip is the Minister of Parliamentary Affairs.

statements.t: Though not in the Constitution, the Whip has been incorporated in the Rules of the House by the 1998 Facilities Act.
statements.d: incorporated in the Rules of the House
statements.fact: Not in the Constitution – true; but not incorporated in the Rules of the House either; the 1998 Act only provides facilities.

official_questions.stem:
In the context of distinctions existing between a Public Bill and a Private Bill, select the statement/statements that is/are valid :
I. A Private Bill which has been introduced by a Member of Parliament sitting in the opposition and which has been approved by the House will have to be referred to the law department for consultation.
II. A Public Bill is always introduced in the Parliament by the Minister or a member of the government party.
III. A Private Bill will not reflect the policy of the government but upon its approval by the House, a Private Bill would have reflected the policy of the government.
IV. Public Bills and Private Bills, regardless of the differences between them, are governed by the same general procedure, and are required to be passed through the same stages in the House.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: Public (government) bills are introduced only by ministers, drafted by the department in consultation with the Law Ministry and reflect government policy; private members' bills are introduced by non-minister MPs (any party), drafted by the member, and do not reflect government policy even if passed; both follow the same general stages.

statements.t: A private bill introduced by an opposition MP and approved by the House must be referred to the law department for consultation.
statements.fact: Law-ministry consultation in drafting applies to government (public) bills; a private bill is drafted by the member.

statements.t: A public bill is always introduced by a minister or a member of the government party.
statements.d: or a member of the government party
statements.fact: Public bills are introduced only by ministers; a non-minister of the ruling party introduces a private member's bill.

statements.t: A private bill does not reflect government policy but on approval it would reflect government policy.
statements.d: upon its approval ... reflected the policy of the government
statements.fact: A private bill does not reflect government policy – and its passage does not change that.

statements.t: Public and private bills are governed by the same general procedure and pass through the same stages.

official_questions.rule: Public bill = minister; private member's bill = non-minister MP of any party (Fridays); last private bill passed by both Houses: 1970 (LS).
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only.

official_questions.stem:
Which of the following State Bill/Bills will have to be mandatorily reserved for the President's consideration ?
I. A Bill that proposes to give effect to certain Directive Principles of State Policy.
II. A Bill requiring prior Presidential sanction but which was however not obtained under Article 304.
III. A Bill that attracts the provisions of Article 288.
IV. A Bill seeking to operate a provision that belongs to one of the Concurrent List entries, but which is however repugnant to any Union law.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: Mandatory reservation: bills derogating from High Court powers (Art. 200 proviso) and, in effect, Art. 288(2) bills taxing water/electricity of Union authorities (no effect without reservation and assent); reservation for DPSP laws (Art. 31C), Art. 304(b) and Art. 254(2) is optional (needed only for protection/validity).

statements.t: A State bill giving effect to certain DPSP must mandatorily be reserved for the President.
statements.fact: DPSP bills are reserved only if Art. 31C protection is sought – optional.

statements.t: A State bill requiring prior Presidential sanction under Art. 304 that was not obtained must be mandatorily reserved.
statements.fact: Missing Art. 304(b) previous sanction can be cured by later assent (Art. 255); reservation is not mandatory.

statements.t: A State bill attracting Article 288 must be reserved for the President.
A State bill on a Concurrent entry repugnant to Union law must mandatorily be reserved.
statements.fact: Art. 254(2) reservation is optional – the State reserves only if it wants the law to prevail.

official_questions.rule: Mandatory: HC-derogating bill (Art. 200), Art. 288(2); optional: 31A/31C, 254(2), 304(b).
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only.

official_questions.stem:
In the context of Centre - State Relations, which of the following statement/statements are valid ?
I. Punchhi Commission had recommended that the procedure that is followed for the removal of President should also be applicable for the impeachment of Governors as well.
II. The law that is made by the Parliament with respect to any matter in the State List in relation to the State in which President's rule is imposed, cannot be re-enacted by the State Legislature after the President's rule is ended.
III. The Sarkaria Commission was not the first to recommend the establishment of an Inter-State Council.
IV. Only the Lok Sabha can pass a resolution declaring that it is necessary in the national interest that the Parliament should make laws with respect to Goods and Services Tax.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: Punchhi (2010): Governor removable by impeachment-like procedure as for the President; Art. 357(2): laws made during President's rule continue until altered by the State legislature; ARC (1969) recommended an ISC before Sarkaria; Art. 249 resolutions (incl. GST, Art. 246A) are passed by Rajya Sabha.

statements.t: Punchhi recommended that the President's removal procedure be applied to impeachment of Governors.
statements.d: procedure ... for the removal of President

statements.t: A Parliament law on a State subject during President's rule cannot be re-enacted by the State legislature afterwards.
statements.fact: Art. 357(2): such laws continue until altered, repealed or amended by the State legislature – which it can do.

statements.t: The Sarkaria Commission was not the first to recommend an Inter-State Council.
Only the Lok Sabha can pass a resolution letting Parliament legislate on GST in the national interest.
statements.fact: Art. 249 resolutions (including GST matters) are passed by the Rajya Sabha.

official_questions.rule: Art. 249 = Rajya Sabha 2/3 (also GST under 246A); ISC first urged by ARC 1969, then Rajamannar, Sarkaria; set up 1990.
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only. Statement II is worded oddly ('re-enacted'), but Art. 357(2) lets the State alter/repeal such laws.

official_questions.stem:
In the context of the enactment of Budget, which of the following statement/statements is/are valid ?
I. The Appropriation Bill carries an automatic repeal clause.
II. The provision 'Vote on Account' has become ineffectual after the re-scheduling of the budget cycle from the last day of February to the first day of February.
III. Amendments to either reject or reduce a tax can not be moved in case of the Finance Bill.
IV. The expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India can only be discussed.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: Appropriation Act authorises spending for the year and lapses with it (key: 'automatic repeal'); vote on account (Art. 116) is still used, e.g. in election years; on a Finance Bill amendments to reduce or abolish a tax can be moved (increase needs recommendation); charged expenditure is discussed but not voted (Art. 113(1)).

statements.t: The Appropriation Bill carries an automatic repeal clause.
Vote on account has become ineffectual after the budget moved to 1 February.
statements.fact: Vote on account is still used (interim budgets in election years); the 1 Feb budget reduced, not abolished, its need.

statements.t: Amendments to reject or reduce a tax cannot be moved on the Finance Bill.
statements.fact: Amendments to reduce or abolish a tax can be moved on the Finance Bill.

statements.t: Expenditure charged on the Consolidated Fund of India can only be discussed.

official_questions.rule: Charged = discussed, not voted; Finance Bill: reduce/abolish tax amendments allowed; vote on account still used.
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only. Statement I is the key's wording; strictly the Appropriation Act exhausts with the financial year.

official_questions.stem:
In connection with the veto power of the Indian President, which one of the following statement/statements is/are valid ?
I. The Indian President possesses 'Suspensive Veto' in the case of Money Bills but not in the case of Finance Bills.
II. The Indian President can exercise 'Absolute Veto' with respect to the Government Bills at all times.
III. The Indian President enjoys 'Pocket Veto' indefinitely whereas the American President possesses 'Qualified Veto'.
IV. The objective of the veto power in being conferred upon the Indian President is to ensure a system of checks and balances between the office of the President and that of the power of the Parliament.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: President: absolute veto (private members' bills, or govt resigned before assent), suspensive veto (ordinary bills, not Money Bills), pocket veto (no time limit); US President: qualified veto overridable by 2/3 of Congress; veto aims to prevent hasty or unconstitutional legislation.

statements.t: The President has a suspensive veto in case of Money Bills but not Finance Bills.
statements.d: 'Suspensive Veto' in the case of Money Bills
statements.fact: The President has no suspensive veto over Money Bills (only assent or withhold).

statements.t: The President can exercise absolute veto on Government bills at all times.
statements.fact: Absolute veto is used only in specific cases (private members' bills; cabinet resigned before assent).

statements.t: The Indian President enjoys pocket veto indefinitely whereas the American President possesses qualified veto.
The objective of the veto is checks and balances between the President and Parliament.
statements.fact: Per key: the objective is to prevent hasty and ill-considered or unconstitutional legislation, not a President-Parliament power balance.

official_questions.rule: India: absolute, suspensive, pocket (no qualified); USA: qualified + pocket (10 days).
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only.

official_questions.stem: Which of the following statement is correct regarding Parliamentary Privileges ?
options: Parliamentary Privileges are the privileges that are enjoyed collectively by each House of the Parliament, and not by the Members individually.
Only Members can be punished for contempt by reprimand and admonition but not outsiders.
The phrase 'Breach of Privilege' has wider implications than the 'Contempt of the House'.
The Members cannot be arrested during the session of Parliament but this privilege is available only in civil cases and not in criminal cases or preventive detention cases.
official_questions.key: The Members cannot be arrested during the session of Parliament but this privilege is available only in civil cases and not in criminal cases or preventive detention cases.
official_questions.core_fact: Privileges are collective and individual; freedom from arrest during session and 40 days before/after applies only in civil cases; Houses can punish members and outsiders for contempt; 'contempt of the House' is wider than 'breach of privilege'.

statements.t: Parliamentary privileges are enjoyed collectively by each House and not by Members individually.
statements.d: collectively ... not by the Members individually
statements.fact: Privileges are enjoyed both collectively and individually.

statements.t: Only Members, not outsiders, can be punished for contempt by reprimand and admonition.
statements.fact: Outsiders too can be punished for contempt (reprimand, admonition, imprisonment).

statements.t: 'Breach of privilege' has wider implications than 'contempt of the House'.
statements.fact: Contempt of the House is the wider expression; breach of privilege is narrower.

statements.t: Members cannot be arrested during session, but only in civil cases – not criminal or preventive detention.

official_questions.rule: Freedom from arrest: civil only, session + 40 days before/after; privileges collective + individual; contempt ⊃ breach of privilege.
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only.

official_questions.stem:
The equal status of the Rajya Sabha with the Lok Sabha can be described by which of the following statement/statements ?
I. Introduction and passage of Money Bills.
II. Consideration of the CAG's report.
III. Initiating the removal of the Vice-President.
IV. Approval of proclamation of all the three types of emergencies by the President.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: Rajya Sabha has equal powers in considering CAG/constitutional bodies' reports and approving all three emergencies; unequal on Money Bills (LS only); VP removal resolution can originate only in Rajya Sabha (special power).

statements.t: Rajya Sabha has equal status with Lok Sabha in introduction and passage of Money Bills.
statements.d: Introduction and passage of Money Bills
statements.fact: Money Bills can be introduced only in the Lok Sabha; RS has unequal power.

statements.t: Rajya Sabha has equal status in considering the CAG's report.
Rajya Sabha has equal status with Lok Sabha in initiating removal of the Vice-President.
statements.d: Initiating the removal of the Vice-President
statements.fact: VP removal can be initiated only in Rajya Sabha – a special power, not equality.

statements.t: Rajya Sabha has equal status in approving all three types of emergencies.
statements.d: all the three types of emergencies

official_questions.rule: RS equal: ordinary/constitutional bills, President's election/impeachment, emergencies, reports; unequal: Money Bills, no-confidence; special: 249, 312, VP removal start.
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only.

official_questions.stem:
Which of the following source/sources of revenue qualifies/qualify for being given to the Panchayats ?
I. The tax proceeds that are assigned to the States from the Centre may be again re-distributed to the Panchayats as recommended by the Central Finance Commission.
II. Loans from the State Government.
III. Under Article 243-I of the Constitution of India, the State Government is empowered to devolve its own funds to the Panchayats even in the absence of the State Finance Commission's recommendations.
IV. Internal Resource Generation is facilitated only in the case of Panchayats situated in Scheduled Areas as per the Fifth Schedule.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: Panchayats get: taxes/fees assigned by State law (243H), grants, State loans, own revenue (all tiers, not only Scheduled Areas); devolution of State taxes follows the SFC (243-I); the Central FC only recommends measures to augment the State's CF to supplement Panchayat resources (280(3)(bb)).

statements.t: Tax proceeds assigned to States may be redistributed to Panchayats as recommended by the Central Finance Commission.
statements.d: as recommended by the Central Finance Commission
statements.fact: Redistribution to Panchayats follows the SFC; the Central FC recommends measures to augment the State Consolidated Fund.

statements.t: Loans from the State Government are a source of Panchayat revenue.
Under Art. 243-I the State can devolve its own funds to Panchayats even without SFC recommendations.
statements.d: Under Article 243-I ... even in the absence of the SFC
statements.fact: Per key: Art. 243-I concerns the SFC's review; devolution powers come from State law under 243H.

statements.t: Internal resource generation is facilitated only for Panchayats in Fifth Schedule areas.
statements.d: only in the case of Panchayats situated in Scheduled Areas
statements.fact: Internal resource generation is available to all Panchayats, not only Scheduled Areas.

official_questions.rule: Panchayat finance: 243H (State law assigns taxes/grants), 243-I (SFC), 280(3)(bb) (CFC augments State CF).
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only.

official_questions.stem:
In connection with the lapsing of Bills, which of the following statement/statements is/are valid ?
I. If the Lok Sabha has passed the Bill, but if the Bill has still not been discussed in the Rajya Sabha, then such a Bill does not lapse.
II. A Bill returned by the President for reconsideration of the Houses will not lapse. However, the Lok Sabha should not have been dissolved by the time the Bill is returned.
III. A Bill that is passed by both the Houses but pending for President's assent will not lapse.
IV. A Bill that is pending in the Rajya Sabha but which has not been passed by the Lok Sabha will also lapse.
Select the correct answer using the codes given below :
official_questions.core_fact: On LS dissolution: bills pending in LS lapse; bills passed by LS but pending in RS lapse; bills pending in RS not passed by LS do not lapse; bills passed by both Houses awaiting assent do not lapse; bills returned by the President do not lapse; bills notified for joint sitting do not lapse.

statements.t: A bill passed by LS but not yet discussed in RS does not lapse.
statements.fact: A bill passed by LS and pending in RS lapses.

statements.t: A bill returned by the President does not lapse, provided the LS was not dissolved by then.
statements.d: However, the Lok Sabha should not have been dissolved
statements.fact: A bill returned by the President does not lapse even if the LS has been dissolved.

statements.t: A bill passed by both Houses and pending assent does not lapse.
statements.d: pending for President's assent will not lapse

statements.t: A bill pending in RS but not passed by LS also lapses.
statements.fact: A bill pending in RS and not passed by LS does not lapse.

official_questions.rule: Lapse test: is the bill 'in' or 'from' the Lok Sabha? LS-originated pending bills lapse; RS-pending (non-LS) bills, assent-pending, returned, joint-sitting-notified bills survive.
official_questions.key_note: Initial key only.
